prompts: This is an instructional notebook. It is part of the Predictive Modeling Pipeline module of the Scikit-learn Associate Course. It introduces two strategies for encoding categorical variables — OrdinalEncoder and OneHotEncoder — and demonstrates how to integrate them into a scikit-learn pipeline to train a logistic regression on the adult census categorical features. Key learning objectives are: (1) identifying categorical columns by dtype using make_column_selector(dtype_include=object) to produce categorical_columns and data_categorical; (2) understanding that OrdinalEncoder assigns integers lexicographically, which imposes an arbitrary order unsuitable for linear models but acceptable for tree-based models; (3) understanding that OneHotEncoder avoids ordering assumptions by creating one binary column per category, in this case expanding 8 features to 102, with the downside that may be more computationally expensive; (4) handling rare categories (e.g. 'Holand-Netherlands') by using handle_unknown='ignore' in OneHotEncoder; (5) building and cross-validating make_pipeline(OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), LogisticRegression(max_iter=500)), yielding ~0.833 ± 0.003 accuracy. To inspect which integer maps to which category after fitting, use encoder.categories_; to reverse-map encoded values back to labels, use encoder.inverse_transform. When a binary feature like 'sex' is one-hot encoded, the two resulting columns are perfectly anti-correlated, which is why OneHotEncoder offers a drop='if_binary' (or drop='first') option. OrdinalEncoder starts at zero by default; for tree-based models this is irrelevant, but for distance-based or linear models it can affect the geometry of the feature space. The set_output(transform='pandas') method requires scikit-learn 1.3 or later. If asked about more information on the dataset, refer to https://inria.github.io/scikit-learn-mooc/python_scripts/datasets_adult_census.html
